sections.heading: Overshoot from RHPZ
sections.text: In boost-mode operation (V_out > V_in), the buck-boost has an RHPZ identical to a boost converter. If overshoot occurs in this region, reduce voltage-loop crossover below f_RHPZ/4. In buck-mode (V_out < V_in), there is no RHPZ — overshoot is a pure gain/tuning issue.

sections.heading: Slow settling from operating-point shift
sections.text: The buck-boost plant dynamics change significantly between buck and boost modes. If settling is slow near the buck-boost boundary (V_out ~ V_in), the controller must handle the transition. Cascaded current-mode with gain scheduling is the robust solution.

sections.heading: Excess ripple from duty-cycle range
sections.text: At extreme duty cycles (very high or very low D), the inductor current ripple increases. Verify the inductor sizing is adequate for the worst-case operating point. Controller gain changes will not fix ripple from undersized passives.

sections.heading: Efficiency from conduction losses
sections.text: Buck-boost efficiency is inherently lower than buck or boost alone because the current path always includes both the switch and the diode (or synchronous rectifier). The controller cannot improve this — consider a different topology if efficiency is critical.

sections.heading: Architecture limit
sections.text: If the buck-boost fails transient specs across the full operating range, the plant dynamics are too variable for a fixed-gain controller. Consider: (1) gain scheduling based on duty cycle, (2) cascaded current-mode, or (3) a different topology if the conversion ratio is always step-down or always step-up.
